questions.question: An $M/M/1$ queue has Poisson arrivals with rate $\lambda$, exponential service with rate $\mu$, one server and unlimited waiting room, and load $\rho=\lambda/\mu$. For which loads does the number in the system have a stationary distribution?
options: For every $\rho>0$, since unlimited waiting room means no job is ever lost
For $\rho\leq1$, since a server that keeps up with arrivals on average suffices
For $\rho<1$, since only then the normalising sum $\sum_{n\geq0}\rho^n$ is finite
For every $\rho\neq1$, since the closed form $\sum_{n\geq0}\rho^n=1/(1-\rho)$ is defined whenever $\rho\neq1$

questions.question: In a stable $M/M/1$ queue with load $\rho=\lambda/\mu<1$, which long-run quantity equals $\rho$ itself?
options: The mean number of jobs in service, $\mathbb{E}[L_s]$
The mean number of jobs in the system, $\mathbb{E}[L]$
The mean number of jobs waiting in queue, $\mathbb{E}[Q]$
The long-run fraction of time the system is empty

questions.question: An $M/M/1$ queue is modelled as a birth-death queue with departure rate $\mu(n)=\mu$ for every $n\geq1$ jobs present. Why does exponential service with rate $\mu$ justify a departure rate that ignores how long the current service has lasted?
options: Poisson arrivals make the departure process Poisson with rate $\mu$ at every queue length.
The remaining service time of the job in service is again exponential with rate $\mu$.
Under FCFS the job in service is the oldest one, so its remaining time is fixed at $1/\mu$.
Any service distribution with mean $1/\mu$ completes jobs at rate $\mu$ at every moment.

questions.question: In a stable $M/M/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda$, mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$, why does the long-run fraction of time the server is busy equal $\rho$?
options: Exponential service times are what make the busy fraction equal to the load.
Arriving jobs see the server busy with probability $\rho$, and that is what defines the load.
Any single-server queue with $\rho<1$ has busy fraction $\rho$, also when jobs are blocked.
Every arriving job is admitted and served, so work arrives and is completed at rate $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$.

questions.question: In a stable $M/M/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda$, service rate $\mu$ and stationary probabilities $p(n)$, the recursion $p(n+1)=\rho\,p(n)$ with $\rho=\lambda/\mu$ comes from equating the rate of jumps from level $n$ up to $n+1$ with the rate of jumps from $n+1$ down to $n$. Which equation is this?

Customers arrive at a single desk, modelled as an $M/M/1$ queue, at rate $\lambda=9$ per hour, and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=5$ minutes. What is the mean number of customers in the system, $\mathbb{E}[L]$?
A stable $M/M/1$ queue has load $\rho=0.6$. What is the long-run fraction of time during which more than two jobs are in the system, $\mathbb{P}(L>2)$?
A stable $M/M/1$ queue has load $\rho=0.9$, so the mean number in the system is $\mathbb{E}[L]=9$. What is the mean number of jobs waiting in queue (not in service), $\mathbb{E}[Q]$?

Jobs arrive at an $M/M/1$ queue at rate $\lambda=10$ per hour and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=4$ minutes, so the mean number in the system is $\mathbb{E}[L]=2$. What is the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ (waiting plus service)?
A stable $M/M/1$ queue has load $\rho=0.8$. What is the variance of the number in the system, $\operatorname{Var}(L)$?
In a stable $M/M/1$ queue under first-come first-served with arrival rate $\lambda$, service rate $\mu$ and load $\rho=\lambda/\mu<1$, which description of the waiting time in queue $W$ is correct?
options: $W$ is exponential with rate $\mu(1-\rho)$, so $\mathbb{P}(W>x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\mu(1-\rho)x}$ for $x\geq0$.
$W$ is exponential with rate $\mu$, since a waiting job waits for one service to finish.
$W$ is geometric, $\mathbb{P}(W=n)=(1-\rho)\rho^n$, like the number of jobs an arrival finds.
$\mathbb{P}(W=0)=1-\rho$, and given $W>0$ the wait is exponential with rate $\mu(1-\rho)$.

questions.question: In Probability Theory, $X\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)$ counts the failures before the first success, $\mathbb{P}(X=k)=(1-p)^kp$ for $k\geq0$, and $\operatorname{FS}(p)$ counts the trials up to and including the first success. Which law has the number in the system $L$ of a stable $M/M/1$ queue with load $\rho$?

In a stable $M/M/1$ queue with load $\rho$, the service order is changed from first-come first-served to random order of service, with $\lambda$ and $\mu$ unchanged. Which of these results relies on the FCFS order and may fail after the change?
options: $\mathbb{P}(W>x)=\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mu(1-\rho)x}$ for the waiting time $W$ in queue
$p(n)=(1-\rho)\rho^n$ for the long-run fraction of time with $n$ jobs present
The long-run fraction of time the server is busy equals $\rho$
An arriving job finds $n$ jobs present with probability $p(n)$

questions.question: Calls arrive at $\lambda=81$ per hour and each takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=2$ minutes. A manager treats $c$ agents as one $M/M/1$ server working $c$ times as fast, so $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]/c$. What is the smallest $c$ for which the mean number of calls in the system is $\mathbb{E}[L]\leq3$?

Customers arrive at an $M/M/1$ queue under FCFS at rate $\lambda=6$ per hour and are served at rate $\mu=10$ per hour. What is the probability that an arriving customer waits in queue longer than $15$ minutes?

An office modelled as a stable $M/M/1$ queue with load $\rho=0.8$ has $3$ seats for waiting customers; the customer in service does not need a seat. What is the long-run fraction of time in which every waiting customer can sit?

Calls arrive as a Poisson process at rate $\lambda$ to $c\geq2$ agents, each serving at exponential rate $\mu$ from one shared line, with $\lambda<c\mu$. A planner instead uses one $M/M/1$ server with rate $c\mu$. How does this approximation compare with the actual mean number in the system?
options: It underestimates it: with $n<c$ calls present the agents work at total rate $n\mu<c\mu$, while the fast server always uses $c\mu$.
It is exact: both systems have total service capacity $c\mu$ and the same load $\lambda/(c\mu)$, so their $\mathbb{E}[L]$ agree.
It overestimates it: $c$ agents serve several calls at once, so no call waits behind a long call, unlike at one fast server.
It overestimates it: one fast server has a single long line, while $c$ agents each keep their own shorter line.

questions.question: A clinic is to be modelled as an $M/M/1$ queue. Long-run data show that the server is idle $45\%$ of the time, but only $30\%$ of arriving patients find the server idle. What do these data imply for the $M/M/1$ model?
options: They fit it: arrivals tend to come when others are present, so they find the server idle less often than an outside observer.
They fit it if service is not FCFS: the order of service decides how often an arrival finds the server idle.
They fit it if service is not exponential: Poisson arrivals alone do not make the two fractions agree.
They contradict it: with Poisson arrivals both fractions would equal the time-average idle probability $p(0)$.

questions.question: A stable $M/M/1$ queue has service rate $\mu=10$ per hour and arrival rate $\lambda=9$ per hour, so $\mathbb{E}[L]=9$. With $\mu$ fixed, to which arrival rate must $\lambda$ be lowered so that the mean number in the system halves to $\mathbb{E}[L]=4.5$?

Design A: two clerks each run their own $M/M/1$ queue with arrival rate $4$ per hour and service rate $5$ per hour. Design B: one clerk twice as fast (rate $10$ per hour) serves all $8$ arrivals per hour as one $M/M/1$ queue. What are the mean sojourn times $\mathbb{E}[J]$ in A and B?
